notes: Werner-Schaus II (since Feb 1969): CSV in ruling slot 1 (moved from MD slot 14, keeps its MD sprite LUX_non_aligned_conservative) and DP in coalition slot 2. Slot 14 holds the Catholic diocese. Radical left from the ASSOSS/GSR milieu: Trotskyist minority in slot 5 (becomes the LCR on 1970.9.5), Maoist GSR majority in slot 19. Slot 20 is the forcibly-conscripted veterans' protest movement (MIP merged into DP in 1968). LUX_western_conservative (ADR sprite) unused.

0.name: Service de Renseignement de l'État
0.text:
The State Intelligence Service was created by law in 1960 and reports directly to the Prime Minister. Small but well connected, it watches the Communist Party and its steel-town cells, keeps an eye on Soviet bloc diplomats and trade missions, and works closely with Belgian, French, West German and American services in a country that hosts NATO's maintenance and supply agency at Capellen. In great secrecy it also oversees Luxembourg's stay-behind network, prepared to organise resistance under a Soviet occupation.

The service embodies Luxembourg's postwar choice: after two German occupations, security lies only in the Atlantic Alliance. Anti-communist, discreet and loyal to the Grand Duke, it would anchor any government that put order and Western solidarity above parliamentary routine.

1.name: Chrëschtlech Sozial Vollekspartei
1.text:
The Christian Social People's Party is Luxembourg's natural party of government and has led every cabinet since the Second World War. Prime Minister Pierre Werner, in office since 1959 and also minister of finance, has governed since early 1969 in coalition with the Democratic Party after dropping the socialists, while Jean Dupong presides over the party. In the December 1968 election it won 21 of the 56 seats.

Rooted in the Catholic Church, the Christian trade union LCGB, the farmers and the daily Luxemburger Wort, the CSV combines Catholic social teaching with a market economy and a generous welfare state. It is firmly Atlanticist and federalist in Europe: Werner has long argued for monetary union, which the Hague summit of December 1969 has placed on the Community's agenda.

2.name: Demokratesch Partei
2.text:
The Democratic Party is Luxembourg's liberal party, heir to the patriotic and liberal groupings formed after the liberation. Under Gaston Thorn it rose to eleven seats in 1968 after absorbing the protest movement of the forcibly conscripted, and since February 1969 it has governed with the CSV: Thorn is foreign minister and Eugène Schaus deputy prime minister.

The DP stands for individual freedom, private enterprise, secular schools and a modern, efficient state, and it speaks for the civil servants, professionals, shopkeepers and anticlerical middle classes of the capital, where it is strongest. Pro-European and Atlanticist, it backs the growth of the financial centre and hopes to turn its role as kingmaker into lasting influence over the CSV-dominated state.

3.name: Lëtzebuerger Sozialistesch Aarbechterpartei
3.text:
The Luxembourg Socialist Workers' Party, founded in 1902 as the Social Democratic Party, is the party of the steel towns of the Minett and of the socialist trade unions. After five years in coalition with the CSV it was pushed into opposition in 1969 despite holding 18 seats, and its former deputy prime minister Henry Cravatte leads a party divided between a moderate right and an increasingly militant left.

The LSAP defends automatic wage indexation, social security, public investment and secular education, and it backs NATO and European integration. Its left wing, strong among young militants and steelworkers, wants cooperation with the communists in the town halls of the south and a sharper anti-capitalist line, which the party's right around Cravatte rejects outright. Its base is the LAV union.

4.name: Kommunistesch Partei vu Lëtzebuerg
4.text:
The Communist Party of Luxembourg, founded in 1921, enjoys its best result since the war: 15.5 percent and six seats in December 1968, won in the steel towns of Esch-sur-Alzette, Differdange, Dudelange and Rumelange. It is led by Dominique Urbany, publishes the daily Zeitung vum Lëtzebuerger Vollek and has a solid base in the unions of the Minett.

The KPL is among the most loyal pro-Soviet parties in Western Europe and endorsed the 1968 Warsaw Pact intervention in Czechoslovakia. It calls for nationalisation of the steel industry, higher wages, better housing and withdrawal from NATO, and it denounces the EEC as a cartel of monopolies. Its leverage lies in the industrial south, where it competes with the socialists for the loyalty of the steelworkers.

5.name: D'Trotzkisten
5.text:
The Trotskyists are the minority inside the Revolutionary Socialist Left, the radical movement born in 1969 from the old General Association of Luxembourg Students. Luxembourg has no full university, so its young radicals were formed abroad, in Paris, Brussels and the German university towns of 1968, where they were won over by Ernest Mandel's Fourth International and Alain Krivine's new Ligue communiste.

They reject both the Soviet bureaucracy embodied by the KPL and the Maoist cult of the GSR majority, preaching permanent revolution, workers' councils and solidarity with the Vietnamese and Latin American guerrillas. Few in number, they are energetic pamphleteers in the lycées and among young steelworkers, and they chafe at sharing an organisation with the Maoists.

5.name: Ligue Communiste Révolutionnaire
5.text:
The Revolutionary Communist League was founded on 5 September 1970 by the Trotskyist minority of the Revolutionary Socialist Left after the majority turned to Maoism. Linked to the Fourth International, it counts among its leading members Robert Engel, Jhemp Lulling and Marc Reckinger, and it publishes its own paper.

The LCR fights for a socialist Europe of workers' councils, against both NATO and the Soviet bureaucracy, and backs anti-imperialist movements from Vietnam to Latin America. It works in schools, among apprentices and in the steel unions, and supports every strike it can reach. Small and largely middle-class in origin, it is nonetheless one of the most active forces on Luxembourg's revolutionary left.

6.name: D'Neutralisten
6.text:
The Neutralists are a scattering of elderly notables, Catholic traditionalists and nationalist veterans who never accepted the constitutional revision of 1948 that struck out Luxembourg's 'perpetual neutrality', guaranteed by the Treaty of London in 1867, nor the entry into NATO a year later. They gather in veterans' associations and rural parish circles, insisting that the Grand Duchy survives only by staying out of the great powers' quarrels.

They want Luxembourg out of NATO's structures, a halt to a supranational Europe that would dissolve the nation and limits on the immigration of foreign workers. Hostile to American mass culture and the EEC's technocrats, they are open to trade with the East and admired de Gaulle's defiance of Washington. Their weight is small, but they voice an old instinct for survival.

7.name: Moskauer Linn
7.text:
The Moscow Line is the hard core of the communist apparatus: functionaries trained at party schools in Moscow and East Berlin, editors of the party press and steel-town cadres who owe their careers to the Soviet connection. In 1968 they made sure the KPL stood with the Warsaw Pact over Czechoslovakia, and they treat any talk of a 'national road' as treason.

They regard parliamentary work as secondary to loyalty to the Soviet Union and would like a neutral Luxembourg tied to the socialist camp, ruled by a vanguard party through the unions and a disciplined security service. Their leverage lies in party finance, the press, the front organisations and the discreet contacts that run through the Soviet embassy in Luxembourg City.

8.name: Usrat Ahl al-Bayt
8.text:
The Family of the Prophet's House is a handful of Lebanese and Iraqi Shia living in Luxembourg: a doctor, a few merchants and students who commute to the universities of Liège and Nancy. Without a mosque, they meet in a private flat in the capital for Muharram readings and send money to schools in south Lebanon.

They follow with admiration Imam Musa al-Sadr, whose Supreme Islamic Shia Council has opened in Beirut to win a fairer share for Lebanon's neglected Shia. Their Islam is moderate, educated and civic: social justice, schools and hospitals, dialogue with Christians and loyalty to the countries that host them. Wary of both the Shah and the Ba'athists in Baghdad, they keep to communal life and have no political weight in the Grand Duchy.

9.name: Maktab-e Najaf
9.text:
The Najaf School is a reading circle of a few Iranian students and trainee engineers from the universities and steelworks of the region around Luxembourg, who meet in the capital to pray and to study the lectures of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf since 1965. Copies of his letters and sermons reach them through pilgrims and Iranian student networks in Germany and France.

The circle holds that the Shah is a tyrant serving America and Israel and that society must be guided by the learned clergy rather than by kings or parliaments. It rejects the secular Iranian opposition abroad as godless and collects religious dues for Khomeini's representatives. Its weight in Luxembourg is nil; its importance lies in the chain of loyalty that binds exiles to Najaf.

10.name: Sandžački džemat
10.text:
The Sandžak Congregation gathers the first few dozen Muslim workers from Yugoslavia's Sandžak and northern Montenegro who have come to Luxembourg's building sites and steel plants. They pray together in a borrowed room on Fridays and at Bayram, and look for guidance to the official Islamic Community of Yugoslavia in Sarajevo, led by Reis-ul-ulema Sulejman Kemura.

Their Islam is traditional, Hanafi and loyal to established authority, whether Tito's federation at home or the Grand Duchy that employs them. They avoid politics, distrust radical preachers and ask only for a burial plot, halal meat and Koran lessons for their children. Their leverage lies in their growing numbers among foreign workers and in the interest of the Yugoslav authorities in keeping them content.

11.name: Usrat al-Tahrir
11.text:
The Tahrir Family is a cell of Jordanian and Palestinian students from Liège and Nancy who meet in Luxembourg City with a few Arab workers of the hotel trade. They spread the ideas of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani and banned in Jordan and most of the Arab world.

They teach that the defeat of 1967 proves the bankruptcy of Arab nationalism and that only a restored caliphate ruling by the sharia can unite the Muslims and liberate Palestine. Democracy, socialism and Western capitalism are all rejected as man-made systems. Disciplined and secretive, they have almost no audience in Luxembourg, but each member is trained to carry the call wherever he settles.

12.name: Halqat al-Ikhwan
12.text:
The Brotherhood Circle is a small study group of Syrian, Egyptian and North African Muslims in Luxembourg: technicians, students and a few employees of the international organisations. They look to the Syrian Muslim Brotherhood leader Issam al-Attar, exiled in Aachen, and to Said Ramadan's Islamic Centre in Geneva for guidance, literature and visiting preachers.

The circle preaches an Islam that is complete, educated and socially engaged, the answer to both Nasser's socialism and Western materialism. It condemns the persecution of the Brotherhood in Egypt and Syria, favours constitutional government based on the sharia and stresses education, charity and moral renewal. Its influence is minute, but its members are patient organisers who hope to found the Grand Duchy's first Islamic association.

13.name: Conseil d'État
13.text:
The Council of State is the guardian of Luxembourg's legal order. Its 21 members, jurists, senior officials and notables appointed by the Grand Duke, examine every bill before the Chamber votes on it, and its litigation committee acts as the country's supreme administrative court. Without its consent the Chamber cannot dispense with the second constitutional vote on a law, which gives it a real suspensive power.

The Council embodies government by experts and notables rather than parties: cautious, legalistic and devoted to continuity, the monarchy and the authority of the state. Its members are drawn from the political and legal establishment, but it prides itself on standing above party quarrels. In a crisis it is the natural body around which a non-partisan administration could be formed.

14.name: Diocèse de Luxembourg
14.text:
The Diocese of Luxembourg, created in 1870, embraces a population that is almost entirely Catholic. Bishop Léon Lommel, in office since 1956, presides over a church whose priests are paid by the state, whose clergy teach religion in the schools and whose printing house publishes the Luxemburger Wort, the country's largest daily. The Octave of Our Lady of Luxembourg and the Echternach dancing procession remain mass events.

The Church backs the CSV and the Christian unions but speaks in its own name on family, schooling and morality: it resists the liberalisation of divorce and the permissive society, while urging social justice for workers and immigrants in the spirit of the Second Vatican Council. Its leverage lies in the pulpit, the press and the loyalty of the countryside.

15.name: Aciéries Réunies de Burbach-Eich-Dudelange
15.text:
ARBED, formed in 1911 by the merger of three steel companies and shaped by the industrialist Emile Mayrisch, is the economic heart of the Grand Duchy. Since taking over its rival HADIR in 1967 it controls most of Luxembourg's steel output from its plants at Esch, Belval, Dudelange and Differdange, as well as works in the Saar, and it is by far the country's largest employer.

Its directors sit at the centre of Luxembourg's economic establishment, alongside Belgian holding companies and the big banks. ARBED favours social peace through bargaining with the unions, low taxes on industry, free trade within the Community and a strong European Coal and Steel Community. When ARBED speaks on wages, investment or energy, the government listens.

16.name: Association des Banques et Banquiers, Luxembourg
16.native_full: Association des Banques et Banquiers, Luxembourg
16.text:
The Luxembourg Bankers' Association, founded in 1939, speaks for a financial centre in rapid growth. The listing of the first Eurobond on the Luxembourg stock exchange in 1963, the generous holding company law of 1929 and strict banking secrecy are drawing a wave of foreign banks, above all from West Germany, Belgium and Switzerland, eager to operate in the Euromarkets beyond the reach of their own regulators.

The association stands for minimal regulation, low taxation, banking secrecy and free movement of capital, and it lobbies discreetly but effectively in the Ministry of Finance, which under Pierre Werner shares its ambitions. It is Atlanticist and pro-European but jealous of national fiscal sovereignty. Its leverage grows each year as banking becomes the second pillar of the economy after steel.

17.name: Lëtzebuerger Natur- a Vulleschutzliga
17.english: Luxembourg League for the Protection of Nature and Birds
17.text:
The Luxembourg League for the Protection of Nature and Birds, founded in 1920, is the oldest conservation body in the Grand Duchy. Its naturalists ring birds, survey the wetlands of the Moselle and the forests of the Ardennes plateau and lobby for nature reserves. In December 1968 young members from its ranks and from the Friends of Nature co-founded a youth association for the study and conservation of nature, bringing a new activist spirit.

The league warns against the price of industrial growth: smoke and slag from the steelworks of the south, the canalised Moselle, new motorways and the reservoir on the Upper Sûre. It is politically neutral and respectable rather than radical, but it is the seedbed of an environmental awareness that Luxembourg's parties have barely begun to notice.

18.name: Lëtzebuerger Aarbechterverband
18.text:
The Luxembourg Workers' Federation is the largest socialist trade union, heir to the miners' and metalworkers' union founded in 1916 on the eve of the great strikes of 1917. Its strongholds are the steelworks and iron mines of the Minett, and it forms the backbone of the General Confederation of Labour, working in tandem with the LSAP.

The LAV fights for automatic wage indexation, shorter hours, workers' seats on company boards and better pensions, and it plays a central role in the social partnership that keeps strikes rare. Its left wing is impatient with the LSAP's caution and favours united action with communist trade unionists. Its leverage lies in its ability to bring the steel industry, and with it the whole economy, to a halt.

19.name: Gauche Socialiste et Révolutionnaire
19.text:
The Revolutionary Socialist Left was born in 1969 when the General Association of Luxembourg Students, a left-liberal student society dating from 1912, completed its turn to revolutionary politics under the impact of May 1968. Its activists, among them Charles Doerner and Robert Medernach, are students and young graduates formed in the universities of France, Belgium and Germany.

The majority of the GSR now follows Mao Zedong Thought: it denounces the Soviet Union and the KPL as revisionist, calls for a proletarian party built among the steelworkers and immigrant labourers of the Minett, and hails China and Albania as beacons. A Trotskyist minority contests this line. Tiny in numbers, the group is loud in the lycées and at factory gates.

20.name: D'Zwangsrekrutéierten
20.text:
The Forcibly Conscripted are the generation of young Luxembourgers drafted into the Wehrmacht after the German decree of August 1942, which provoked a general strike crushed by executions. Some 12,000 were taken; thousands died or vanished, many in the Soviet camp at Tambov. Their associations remain a powerful lobby, and their anger at the 1959 compensation treaty with West Germany produced the Popular Independent Movement, which won two seats in 1964 before merging into the DP.

They demand recognition as victims of Nazism, full compensation from Bonn and pensions for widows and invalids, and they despise the politicians who settled for less. Patriotic, anti-German and suspicious of the established parties, they form a ready reservoir for populist protest whenever their cause is slighted.

21.name: Die Ewiggestrigen
21.text:
The Men of Yesterday are the remnants of the Volksdeutsche Bewegung, the collaborationist movement that under Damian Kratzenberg preached Luxembourg's 'return to the Reich' during the occupation, and of the Luxembourgers who volunteered for German service. After the liberation thousands were tried and purged, Kratzenberg was executed in 1946, and many of the convinced emigrated to West Germany.

Those who remain keep a low profile, meeting in private and reading the German nationalist press. They deny that Luxembourgers are a nation apart, dream of a Germanic Europe and hate communists and the 'patriots' of the resistance alike. They have no organisation worth the name, but they watch with interest the fortunes of the NPD across the Moselle and the Sûre.

22.name: Armée luxembourgeoise
22.text:
The Luxembourg Army is one of the smallest in NATO. Compulsory military service, introduced after the war, was abolished in 1967, and the army is becoming a volunteer force of a few hundred men based at the Herrenberg barracks in Diekirch. Its officers, trained in Belgium and France, uphold a proud tradition that includes the Luxembourg contingent in the Korean War.

The army has no political ambitions and is wholly subordinate to the government, with the Grand Duke, himself a wartime officer of the Irish Guards, as its commander. Its leverage is symbolic rather than real: it embodies sovereignty, NATO solidarity and the memory of the liberation, and it would matter only if the state and the Gendarmerie were overwhelmed by a crisis.

23.name: Maison de Nassau-Weilbourg
23.text:
The House of Nassau-Weilburg has reigned over the Grand Duchy since 1890. Grand Duke Jean succeeded his mother Charlotte in November 1964; she remains revered as the sovereign who embodied national resistance from exile during the occupation. Jean, a former Irish Guards officer who landed in Normandy, and Grand Duchess Joséphine-Charlotte, a Belgian princess, have five children, the heir being Prince Henri, born in 1955.

Confirmed by the 1919 referendum, the monarchy is the keystone of national identity in a small state surrounded by powerful neighbours. The Grand Duke appoints the government, promulgates the laws and represents the country abroad, but rules through ministers responsible to the Chamber. Republicanism is marginal and confined to the far left.
